cues.text: Hey, welcome back.
Today our first question is not which formula to use, but whether the source
matches that formula.
Put a straight wire on the vertical y axis, extending from minus zero point
three to plus zero point three metres.
Current is five amperes upward.
Our observation point is zero point four metres to the right of the centre.
Apply the right hand rule: the field there points into the page.
Every element of this segment contributes in that direction.
But the wire is finite.
For a symmetric segment, the field magnitude is mu zero times current times
half length, divided by two pi times the perpendicular distance times the
square root of half length squared plus distance squared.
Where does that come from?
Each tiny contribution contains the perpendicular distance divided by source
distance cubed.
Integrating along the wire gives the end position factor.
Here, the end distance is half a metre.
Using mu zero divided by four pi approximately ten to the minus seven in SI
units, the result is one point five microtesla.
The infinite wire formula would give two point five microtesla.
That is too large because it includes current elements that are not in our
segment.
As length grows, the finite result approaches the infinite one.
The rest of a real circuit can also contribute, so we have isolated this
segment.
Now two long wires, both carrying current out of the page.
Put three amperes at x zero and six amperes at x zero point three metres.
Between them, the left wire's field points up and the right wire's field
points
down.
Where can they cancel?
Think for a moment.
Equate three divided by x to six divided by zero point three minus x.
Solving gives x zero point one metres, closer to the weaker current.
At smaller distance, its weaker current can still produce the matching field.
Outside the wires, these field directions agree, so there is no finite
cancellation point there.
Reverse a current and redraw the directions; do not recycle this conclusion
blindly.
Geometry and vectors come before arithmetic.
Now follow a particle rather than the source wire.
Magnetic force is charge times velocity cross magnetic field.
It is perpendicular to velocity.
Ask yourself: can that force increase speed?
No.
Its instantaneous power, force dot velocity, is zero.
A static magnetic field alone changes direction, not kinetic energy.
For entry perpendicular to a uniform field, magnetic force supplies the
centripetal acceleration.
Radius is mass times speed divided by charge magnitude times field.
Use charge magnitude for radius; use charge sign to decide bending direction.
For example, positive charge entering along positive x with field along
positive z initially feels force along negative y.
Oblique entry is even more interesting.
Split velocity into a perpendicular component and a parallel component.
The perpendicular component rotates.
The parallel component stays constant.
Together they make a helix.
Let's calculate one.
Mass is two times ten to the minus twenty seven kilograms.
Charge magnitude is ten to the minus nineteen coulombs.
Field is zero point two tesla.
Perpendicular speed is two times ten to the fifth metres per second, while
parallel speed is ten to the fifth.
The radius is zero point zero two metres, or two centimetres.
We used perpendicular speed, not total speed.
The period is two pi times mass divided by charge magnitude times field,
approximately six point two eight three times ten to the minus seven seconds.
Multiply by parallel speed to get the pitch, zero point zero six two eight
three metres per turn.
Pause: a smaller parallel speed changes pitch but not radius if the
perpendicular speed stays fixed.
Within this nonrelativistic model, period does not depend on speed.
Relativistic motion requires a different treatment.
Our checks are simple: magnetic work is zero, parallel motion is unchanged,
and
each component goes into the correct geometrical quantity.
Let's connect these ideas into a JEE style apparatus.
First accelerate a particle from negligible initial speed through a potential
difference.
It gains kinetic energy equal to charge magnitude times accelerating voltage,
if losses are negligible.
Next send it perpendicularly into a uniform magnetic field.
Combining energy and circular motion gives radius equal to the square root of
two times mass times voltage divided by charge magnitude, all divided by the
field.
Hold charge magnitude, voltage and field fixed.
If mass doubles, what happens to radius?
Take a moment.
It grows by the square root of two, not by two.
The particles did not enter at the same speed after the same accelerating
voltage.
Now check the detector geometry.
If the particle completes a semicircle and lands on the original entry
boundary, the separation from entry is two radii.
A measured diameter is not a radius.
Other detector positions need their own sketch.
Finally, a velocity selector uses crossed electric and magnetic fields.
Choose velocity along positive x, magnetic field along positive z and electric
field along positive y.
The electric force and magnetic force oppose.
Cancellation requires electric field equal to speed times magnetic field, so
selected speed is E divided by B.
For forty thousand volts per metre and zero point two tesla, it is two hundred
thousand metres per second.
The charge factor cancels, and reversing charge reverses both forces.
But a different entry angle does not satisfy this simple scalar condition.
Different masses at the selected speed have different kinetic energies.
Also, an analyzer after a selector has radius proportional to mass at fixed
charge and field, because speed is now fixed.
Compare that with the square root mass scaling after a fixed accelerating
voltage.
Same magnetic equation, different preparation.
That is the key habit: identify the stage, identify what is held fixed, then
choose the equation.
